cues.text: A Priest Among the Reconquista's Prisoners

In 1231, during the long Christian reconquest of Muslim Spain, the Almohad governor of Caravaca, Zeyt Abuzeyt , held among his prisoners a Christian priest, Ginés Pérez Chirinos , whose faith and profession had drawn the ruler's curiosity.
Wishing to see for himself what this captive priest's religion actually involved, Abuzeyt ordered him to celebrate Mass before the assembled court.
Chirinos began the ceremony on a hastily improvised altar.

Partway through, he realized that nothing stood upon it representing the crucified Christ—a serious problem for a priest determined to celebrate the Mass properly, even under the eyes of a captor testing him.

Tradition holds that light suddenly filled the chamber and two angels descended through an open window bearing a cross with two crossbars, setting it upon the altar before vanishing as quickly as they had come.
The earliest written witness to the story was the Franciscan chronicler Gil de Zamora , historian to King St. Ferdinand III of Castile.
He recorded it within a generation of the event, giving the tradition an unusually early source for a medieval account of this kind.
Moved by what he had seen, Abuzeyt and members of his household are said to have sought baptism soon afterward.
Later Christian writers took this conversion as a genuine turning point in Caravaca's own passage from Muslim to Christian rule during these same decades of the Reconquista.
The cross containing its fragment of the True Cross was stolen from its sanctuary on the night of February 13–14, 1934, amid rising anticlerical unrest.
That unrest preceded Spain's Civil War, and the cross has never been recovered.
Pope Pius XII later provided a fresh relic of the True Cross, still housed today in a faithful replica of the original reliquary.
In 1998, Pope St. John Paul II designated Caravaca de la Cruz the fifth Holy City permitted to celebrate a perpetual jubilee.
It joined Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago de Compostela — a lasting recognition for the small Murcian town where a captive priest once found himself, of all things, short a crucifix for his altar.
